To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
individual differences in living standards are important determinants of happiness in Russia and that collective experiences are also important.

1) individual economic status is strongly related to happiness; 2) individual changes in economic status are weakly related to changes in happiness; 3) collective changes in economic status (such as the 1998 crisis) are strongly related to changes in the distribution of individual happiness.

individual differences in living standards, but not individual changes in living standards, explain the distribution of happiness among Russians, and that collective economic experience, but not individual economic status, explains changes in the distribution of Russian happiness over time.

the happiness of Russians is strongly affected by their individual economic status, but that collective economic experience is also important.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Russian people are not as unhappy as they have been made out to be.
the economic status of individuals matters more than the national economic status of the country for happiness in Russia.
the happiness of Russians is determined by both the level of economic wellbeing and the rate of change in that wellbeing, with individual economic status playing a larger role than collective status.
The main takeaway from our work is that
money does, indeed, buy happiness in Russia.
